challenges.opponent_argument: The fraud ruling is vulnerable because appellee never shows the element of justifiable reliance. The fraud authority retrieved here requires a false material representation, intent to mislead, justifiable reliance, and resulting injury. But appellee’s theory is that appellants filed allegedly false mechanic’s liens after appellee had already purchased the property and recorded its deed. That sequence undercuts reliance in any transaction by appellee; the liens may be alleged clouds on title, but they are not a fraud on which appellee relied to acquire the property or enter the transaction.
challenges.why_it_matters: If reliance is missing, the fraud claim cannot stand as a matter of law, and the summary judgment on Count Three falls.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited fraud authority requires justifiable reliance and resulting injury. Appellee’s theory in the brief is that appellants filed false mechanic’s liens after appellee already bought and recorded its deed, which leaves a real gap on reliance: appellee did not rely on the liens to enter the property transaction. The brief tries to recast the recorded liens as the relevant misrepresentation and says reliance was justifiable, but it does not cleanly show who relied on what, or how appellee itself was defrauded in the fraud-count sense. On this record, that omission is a real risk to the fraud summary-judgment ruling, and it could also destabilize punitive damages because the punitive award rides on the fraud finding.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee’s summary-judgment evidence established that Appellants recorded three mechanic’s-lien affidavits containing false statements about supposed contracts and amounts owed, knew those statements were false, and filed the liens to mislead others and cloud title to the Property. Appellants filed no timely evidentiary opposition to that motion. To the extent Appellant argues that appellee had to prove reliance in order to show injury from the false recordings, the record establishes that Appellants’ false public filings caused appellee injury by clouding title and forcing appellee to address and remove the liens. In any event, the trial court’s liability ruling is independently supported by the undisputed slander-of-title evidence.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not try to force the fraud count through without a reliance showing. Either add a record citation proving appellee’s actual reliance if one exists, or narrow the response so the judgment is sustained on the independent slander-of-title theory and the unopposed record, not on a stretched fraud theory.

challenges.opponent_argument: The judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling is overclaimed because lis pendens does not automatically eliminate factual disputes about title; it is a notice doctrine, not a shortcut to adjudicating ownership on the pleadings. The title-issues source emphasizes that title questions turn on present ownership of record title, and the sheriff-deed statutes show the deed process has its own statutory steps. On this record, appellee still had to prove that its title was superior and that appellants’ claimed interests were legally void; the brief’s assertion that lis pendens alone foreclosed any factual issue is too broad to support judgment on the pleadings.
challenges.why_it_matters: If this lands, Assignment of Error II is not defeated by a blanket lis pendens argument, and the court must confront whether the pleadings actually established quiet title as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some legal footing because lis pendens is notice, not an automatic title adjudication. But on this record it likely does not carry the day. The brief does more than invoke lis pendens in the abstract: it ties the mechanic’s liens to admissions that the first work was after the foreclosure filing date, then argues that any later-acquired interest was subject to the foreclosure action and could not be asserted against appellee’s title. The trial court’s judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling is still vulnerable if the appellate court thinks the pleadings did not conclusively establish voidness, but the brief has a direct answer and the admitted dates are a substantial record point in appellee’s favor.
challenges.suggested_response: The judgment on the pleadings did not rest on lis pendens in the abstract. Appellants admitted that the first work identified in their mechanic’s liens occurred on December 1, 2016, after the foreclosure complaint was filed, and the complaint in the foreclosure case had already placed the world on constructive notice of the action. Under R.C. 2703.26 and the authorities cited above, any interest acquired after that filing was subject to the outcome of the foreclosure action and could not be asserted against appellee’s title. On the face of the pleadings, therefore, Appellants could not state a viable basis to defeat appellee’s quiet-title and declaratory-judgment claims.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the lis pendens argument so it does not sound like notice doctrine automatically erases factual disputes. Anchor the ruling in the admitted dates and the rule that interests acquired after the foreclosure filing are subject to the outcome of that action.

challenges.opponent_argument: The standing theory is built on the wrong statute. R.C. 5301.07 is a recording-presumption statute for real property instruments; the sheriff’s deed statutes in R.C. 2329.31 and 2329.36 govern the sale-and-deed process. And the retrieved title-issues source makes the opposite point from appellee’s framing: in Ohio, a deed does not have to be recorded to pass title. So recording plus a corrected notary block does not itself prove marketable title or standing; at most it shows appellee is trying to bootstrap standing from a recording presumption that the cited authorities do not say creates standing.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court accepts this, appellee loses the claim that §5301.07 alone solves standing, and Assignment of Error I becomes a legal-structure problem rather than a factual one.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack points to a real structural weakness: R.C. 5301.07 is a recording-presumption statute, and the deed process itself is governed elsewhere. But the brief does not rely on 5301.07 alone. It also cites the standing rule, judicial-sale cases, and the proposition that the recorded deed created a rebuttable presumption that the instrument was valid, enforceable, and effective. So the authority does support appellee’s broader position that a purchaser at sheriff’s sale who has a recorded deed can have a real property interest. What the attack does best is narrow the brief’s logic: it undermines the claim that recording presumptions by themselves equal standing or marketable title. That is a problem, but not necessarily a reversal on this record.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee had standing when it filed suit because it had already purchased the Property at sheriff’s sale and the sheriff’s deed had been recorded before the Complaint was filed. Under R.C. 5301.07(B)(1), the recorded real property instrument carried a rebuttable presumption that it was valid, enforceable, and effective, and Appellants offered no clear and convincing evidence of fraud, undue influence, duress, forgery, incompetency, or incapacity to rebut that presumption. The later affidavit of matters relating to title did not create appellee’s interest; it merely corrected the scrivener’s error in the acknowledgment. In any event, Ohio law recognizes that a deed need not be recorded to pass title. Appellee therefore had a real property interest in the Property when it commenced this action and had standing to pursue its claims.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the standing argument. Do not say R.C. 5301.07 by itself creates standing or marketable title; instead tie standing to the sheriff’s deed, the sale-confirmation/deed statutes, and the rebuttable presumption of validity, and note that the later affidavit corrected the acknowledgment rather than creating appellee’s interest.

challenges.opponent_argument: Appellee’s own timeline makes its standing argument internally unstable. If title passed when the sheriff’s deed was delivered or recorded, then the later October 10 affidavit was unnecessary. If the affidavit was necessary to make the deed effective, then appellee had not cured the defect when it filed suit on July 6, 2017. The cases the brief quotes distinguish an acknowledgment from the deed itself, but they do not say a later corrective affidavit retroactively creates standing as of the complaint date.
challenges.why_it_matters: This preserves the core point that standing must exist when suit is filed; appellee cannot have it both ways.

The brief says the deed recorded on May 16, 2017 created appellee’s enforceable interest and that the October 10 affidavit merely corrected the notary error. That is the brief’s answer to the timing problem. The opposing point is that if the correction was legally necessary to make the deed effective, appellee may not have had standing when it sued on July 6, 2017. The cited source material does not clearly say the later affidavit retroactively perfects title, so the attack exposes a real timing issue. Still, the brief’s position is that the affidavit confirmed, rather than created, the deed’s effectiveness, and the cited authorities are at least consistent with that view.
challenges.suggested_response: Standing is determined at the commencement of the action, and appellee had already acquired and recorded the sheriff’s deed before it filed the Complaint on July 6, 2017. The October 10, 2017 affidavit did not create appellee’s interest or cure a jurisdictional defect retroactively; it simply corrected the erroneous notary information in the already-recorded deed. The deed itself remained effective, and Appellants identified no statutory ground that would defeat the deed’s presumption of validity or nullify appellee’s interest as of the filing date.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Answer the timing point directly. State that the affidavit was corrective only, that standing is measured when suit is filed, and that appellee’s interest existed before the complaint was filed.

challenges.opponent_argument: The punitive-damages theory also overreaches because the only malice evidence the brief points to is Woods’ allegedly hostile courtroom demeanor. Actual malice, however, must exist in the conduct that supports punitive damages; it is not satisfied by irritation, combativeness, or post hoc trial behavior. The punitive-damages source retrieved here says actual malice is a required predicate and that punitive awards are scrutinized for that predicate and proportionality. Demeanor at trial does not establish that the liens themselves were filed with hatred, ill will, or conscious disregard of a great probability of substantial harm.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the evidence does not prove actual malice in the underlying recording conduct, the jury should never have been asked to decide punitive damages.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some appeal, but it is weaker than the reliance point. Ohio punitive damages require actual malice, and the brief’s reliance on Woods’ allegedly hostile courtroom demeanor is thin if that is the main proof. That said, the brief does not rely on demeanor alone: it also points to knowingly false mechanic’s liens, admissions that no contracts existed, and the jury’s actual malice finding. Those facts are enough to give the trial court a basis to submit punitive damages, even if the demeanor evidence is not itself enough. The attack therefore does not show reversible error on this record, but it does highlight the most vulnerable part of the punitive-damages theory.
challenges.suggested_response: The punitive-damages issue was properly submitted because the record contained evidence from which reasonable minds could find actual malice. Appellants admitted they had no contract with Realty Executives, admitted they had no contract with Huntington National Bank, and failed to produce any contract or other document establishing a contract with the Pooles. Yet they recorded mechanic’s-lien affidavits asserting contracts and money due. From that evidence, the jury could find that Appellants acted with a conscious disregard for Appellee’s rights and with a great probability of causing substantial harm. Woods’ hostile and combative conduct at trial was additional evidence of ill will, not the sole basis for the punitive-damages submission. The trial court therefore did not err in allowing the jury to decide punitive damages.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Recast punitive damages around the underlying record evidence of knowing falsity and conscious disregard, not around Woods’ courtroom demeanor alone. Emphasize that the false lien filings and admissions gave the court a basis to submit punitive damages to the jury.

attacks_proposed.argument: The standing theory is built on the wrong statute. R.C. 5301.07 is a recording-presumption statute for real property instruments; the sheriff’s deed statutes in R.C. 2329.31 and 2329.36 govern the sale-and-deed process. And the retrieved title-issues source makes the opposite point from appellee’s framing: in Ohio, a deed does not have to be recorded to pass title. So recording plus a corrected notary block does not itself prove marketable title or standing; at most it shows appellee is trying to bootstrap standing from a recording presumption that the cited authorities do not say creates standing.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court accepts this, appellee loses the claim that §5301.07 alone solves standing, and Assignment of Error I becomes a legal-structure problem rather than a factual one.

attacks_proposed.argument: Appellee’s own timeline makes its standing argument internally unstable. If title passed when the sheriff’s deed was delivered or recorded, then the later October 10 affidavit was unnecessary. If the affidavit was necessary to make the deed effective, then appellee had not cured the defect when it filed suit on July 6, 2017. The cases the brief quotes distinguish an acknowledgment from the deed itself, but they do not say a later corrective affidavit retroactively creates standing as of the complaint date.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This preserves the core point that standing must exist when suit is filed; appellee cannot have it both ways.

attacks_proposed.argument: The fraud ruling is vulnerable because appellee never shows the element of justifiable reliance. The fraud authority retrieved here requires a false material representation, intent to mislead, justifiable reliance, and resulting injury. But appellee’s theory is that appellants filed allegedly false mechanic’s liens after appellee had already purchased the property and recorded its deed. That sequence undercuts reliance in any transaction by appellee; the liens may be alleged clouds on title, but they are not a fraud on which appellee relied to acquire the property or enter the transaction.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If reliance is missing, the fraud claim cannot stand as a matter of law, and the summary judgment on Count Three falls.

attacks_proposed.argument: The punitive-damages theory also overreaches because the only malice evidence the brief points to is Woods’ allegedly hostile courtroom demeanor. Actual malice, however, must exist in the conduct that supports punitive damages; it is not satisfied by irritation, combativeness, or post hoc trial behavior. The punitive-damages source retrieved here says actual malice is a required predicate and that punitive awards are scrutinized for that predicate and proportionality. Demeanor at trial does not establish that the liens themselves were filed with hatred, ill will, or conscious disregard of a great probability of substantial harm.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the evidence does not prove actual malice in the underlying recording conduct, the jury should never have been asked to decide punitive damages.

attacks_proposed.argument: The judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling is overclaimed because lis pendens does not automatically eliminate factual disputes about title; it is a notice doctrine, not a shortcut to adjudicating ownership on the pleadings. The title-issues source emphasizes that title questions turn on present ownership of record title, and the sheriff-deed statutes show the deed process has its own statutory steps. On this record, appellee still had to prove that its title was superior and that appellants’ claimed interests were legally void; the brief’s assertion that lis pendens alone foreclosed any factual issue is too broad to support judgment on the pleadings.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If this lands, Assignment of Error II is not defeated by a blanket lis pendens argument, and the court must confront whether the pleadings actually established quiet title as a matter of law.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited fraud authority requires justifiable reliance and resulting injury. Appellee’s theory in the brief is that appellants filed false mechanic’s liens after appellee already bought and recorded its deed, which leaves a real gap on reliance: appellee did not rely on the liens to enter the property transaction. The brief tries to recast the recorded liens as the relevant misrepresentation and says reliance was justifiable, but it does not cleanly show who relied on what, or how appellee itself was defrauded in the fraud-count sense. On this record, that omission is a real risk to the fraud summary-judgment ruling, and it could also destabilize punitive damages because the punitive award rides on the fraud finding.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says appellee proved the liens contained false statements, appellants knew they were false, intended to mislead, and that reliance on the recorded affidavits was justifiable, with damages reasonably expected.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research would need to show an Ohio fraud theory that allows reliance based on a recorded cloud on title after acquisition, or that appellee relied on the false liens in some transactionally relevant way.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has some legal footing because lis pendens is notice, not an automatic title adjudication. But on this record it likely does not carry the day. The brief does more than invoke lis pendens in the abstract: it ties the mechanic’s liens to admissions that the first work was after the foreclosure filing date, then argues that any later-acquired interest was subject to the foreclosure action and could not be asserted against appellee’s title. The trial court’s judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling is still vulnerable if the appellate court thinks the pleadings did not conclusively establish voidness, but the brief has a direct answer and the admitted dates are a substantial record point in appellee’s favor.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on R.C. 2703.26 and cases saying interests acquired after lis pendens are subject to the foreclosure outcome, and it says appellants admitted the first work date was after the lis pendens date.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The remaining question is whether the pleadings alone, with those admissions, were enough to support quiet-title and declaratory relief as a matter of law.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack points to a real structural weakness: R.C. 5301.07 is a recording-presumption statute, and the deed process itself is governed elsewhere. But the brief does not rely on 5301.07 alone. It also cites the standing rule, judicial-sale cases, and the proposition that the recorded deed created a rebuttable presumption that the instrument was valid, enforceable, and effective. So the authority does support appellee’s broader position that a purchaser at sheriff’s sale who has a recorded deed can have a real property interest. What the attack does best is narrow the brief’s logic: it undermines the claim that recording presumptions by themselves equal standing or marketable title. That is a problem, but not necessarily a reversal on this record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says standing exists when a party has a real interest in the subject matter, cites R.C. 5301.07 for rebuttable presumptions after delivery and acceptance by the recorder, and cites judicial-sale cases for the proposition that the purchaser’s interest is effective from the sale date.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A court would need additional authority on whether a recorded sheriff’s deed with a corrective affidavit is enough to satisfy standing independent of marketable title.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a fair but not decisive attack. The brief says the deed recorded on May 16, 2017 created appellee’s enforceable interest and that the October 10 affidavit merely corrected the notary error. Still, the brief’s position is that the affidavit confirmed, rather than created, the deed’s effectiveness, and the cited authorities are at least consistent with that view.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says appellee acquired a real property interest when the deed was recorded, and that the notary-block error was corrected later by affidavit; it also says the error did not invalidate the deed absent proof of the statutory rebuttal grounds.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The unresolved issue is whether Ohio treats the corrective affidavit as nunc pro tunc for title purposes or only as evidence of an already-valid deed.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has some appeal, but it is weaker than the reliance point. Ohio punitive damages require actual malice, and the brief’s reliance on Woods’ allegedly hostile courtroom demeanor is thin if that is the main proof. That said, the brief does not rely on demeanor alone: it also points to knowingly false mechanic’s liens, admissions that no contracts existed, and the jury’s actual malice finding. Those facts are enough to give the trial court a basis to submit punitive damages, even if the demeanor evidence is not itself enough. The attack therefore does not show reversible error on this record, but it does highlight the most vulnerable part of the punitive-damages theory.

results.assessment: The brief holds up best on the judgment-on-the-pleadings point and on the general title theory, because it does tie its position to the admitted dates and the foreclosure filing. Its weakest spots are the fraud count and standing: the fraud theory leaves a real gap on justifiable reliance, since the alleged false liens came after appellee already bought and recorded its deed, and the standing argument is vulnerable to the timing problem created by the later corrective affidavit. The punitive-damages discussion is also somewhat thin if it leans too hard on courtroom demeanor, though the admitted false lien filings give it some support.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real standing attack, but the cited authorities do not cleanly say that a scrivener-error deed fails to confer any cognizable interest. The brief already answers most of it: it relies on standing at filing, the sheriff’s deed being recorded before the complaint, R.C. 5301.07’s rebuttable presumptions, and the absence of any rebuttal facts like fraud or forgery. On this record, the attack would only land if the court accepted that a recorded deed plus the statutory presumption is still legally insufficient to show a real interest at commencement; otherwise appellee keeps standing and every downstream merits ruling survives.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s standing argument fails because standing is determined at the commencement of the action, and appellee had already acquired and recorded the Sheriff’s Deed before it filed suit. Once the deed was recorded, R.C. 5301.07 created a rebuttable presumption that the instrument was valid, enforceable, and effective, and Appellant identified no clear and convincing evidence of fraud, undue influence, duress, forgery, incompetency, or incapacity to overcome that presumption. The alleged scrivener’s error in the notary block did not defeat appellee’s recorded property interest or its real interest in the subject matter of this action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the standing discussion to rest on appellee’s recorded sheriff’s deed and the R.C. 5301.07 presumption, not on an unqualified claim of “marketable title.” If you want to keep the standing point as strong as possible, say that appellee had a sufficient real interest at filing and delete any implication that the scrivener’s error was irrelevant to every possible title question.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Dresher and Civ.R. 56(E) require the movant to carry the initial evidentiary burden; a late or absent response by appellants does not automatically entitle appellee to judgment. The brief does say appellee produced evidence and that the trial court refused to consider appellants’ untimely opposition, but it does not fully eliminate the attack that fraud and slander of title still required admissible proof of falsity, intent, reliance, and damages. If the record evidence really establishes those elements through admissions, recorded liens, and affidavits, appellee wins; if not, the summary-judgment ruling is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee satisfied its initial Civ.R. 56 burden with admissible record evidence. The summary-judgment materials showed that appellants recorded mechanic’s-lien affidavits asserting contracts and amounts owed that appellants themselves admitted did not exist as to Realty Executives and Huntington National Bank, and appellants failed to produce any contract documentation for the Pooles. Appellee also submitted evidence that the liens were recorded after the lis pendens date, that the statements in the affidavits were false, and that appellants acted with reckless disregard for appellee’s rights in filing and maintaining the liens. Appellants’ late-filed opposition did not relieve them of their reciprocal burden under Civ.R. 56(E), and their failure to submit timely evidentiary materials left appellee’s proof unrebutted. On this record, reasonable minds could reach only one conclusion: appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on slander of title, and the evidence also supported the fraud claim.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen the summary-judgment section by laying out, element by element, the record evidence appellee used to meet Dresher. Do not rely on appellants’ failure to respond; say instead that appellee supported each claim with admitted and undisputed evidence, and that the untimely opposition could not create a genuine issue of fact.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is directionally plausible but not a strong fit to the record. The brief’s answer is that Civ.R. 12(C) was proper because the pleadings and admitted dates showed appellee’s title interest and appellants’ later-acquired liens were subject to lis pendens. The cited authority on lis pendens does support that later-acquired interests take subject to the pending action, but it does not, by itself, show that a title dispute must go to factual development rather than the pleadings when the key dates and admissions are already in the record. Appellants lose only Counts One and Four if this lands, not the whole case.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court properly granted judgment on the pleadings because, accepting the pleadings and all reasonable inferences as true, no material factual issue remained as to appellee’s quiet-title and declaratory-judgment claims. The pleadings established that appellee acquired and recorded its Sheriff’s Deed before the complaint was filed, while appellants’ own admissions showed that the first work underlying the mechanic’s liens occurred after the lis pendens date. Under R.C. 2703.26, once the foreclosure complaint was filed, third persons were charged with notice of the pending action, and any interest acquired thereafter was taken subject to the outcome of that litigation. On those pleaded facts, appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law declaring the liens void and quieting title.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the Civ.R. 12(C) ruling tied to the pleaded and admitted dates, lis pendens, and the recorded deed; do not argue that the court simply resolved a disputed title question as a matter of abstract law. The point is that, on the pleadings, appellee’s recorded interest predated appellants’ liens and later-acquired interests were subject to the pending foreclosure litigation.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some force, but it overstates the problem. Ohio requires actual malice for punitive damages, and a favorable compensatory ratio does not substitute for proof of malice. Still, the brief does not rely only on courtroom demeanor; it also points to the allegedly false mechanic’s-lien affidavits, the intent to mislead, the directed-verdict ruling, and the jury’s actual malice finding. On this record, the hostility evidence is at most corroborative, not the sole basis for punitive damages. Appellants risk losing only the punitive-damages assignment, not the underlying liability findings.
challenges.suggested_response: The punitive-damages award was proper because appellee presented evidence from which the jury could find actual malice. Appellants filed three mechanic’s-lien affidavits containing false statements about supposed contracts and amounts owed, despite the absence of any contract with Realty Executives or Huntington National Bank and despite appellants’ failure to produce contract documentation for the Pooles. The jury was entitled to infer from those false filings and from appellants’ maintenance of the liens after notice of appellee’s interest that appellants acted with a conscious disregard for appellee’s rights. Woods’s hostile and combative conduct during the second phase of trial corroborated the malice evidence; it was not the sole basis for punitive damages. In addition, appellants did not object to the final punitive-damages instructions, and the trial court properly denied their motion for directed verdict. The punitive-damages award bears a reasonable relationship to the compensatory award and was not the product of passion or prejudice.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Reframe punitive damages so the core proof is the false lien filings and the evidence of actual malice, with Woods’s courtroom conduct serving only as corroboration. Keep the waiver point about failure to object to the final instructions, but do not treat that waiver as a substitute for proof of malice.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest on standing and the pleadings ruling: it ties appellee’s interest to a recorded Sheriff’s Deed and leans on lis pendens and the pleaded dates, which gives those issues real traction. The biggest weakness is summary judgment, because the record must still satisfy Dresher and Civ.R. 56(E), and the brief does not fully close the gap on admissible proof of the fraud and slander-of-title elements if the appellants’ late opposition is set aside. Punitive damages are also vulnerable to the extent the proof depends on courtroom hostility rather than the state of mind when the liens were filed, though that point is only partial because the brief also points to false filings and the jury’s malice finding.

challenges.opponent_argument: Land Title’s apparent-authority theory is also incomplete. The brief relies on Kevin Sheridan’s subjective understanding of a private repayment arrangement, but subjective belief does not supply the missing legal link unless it is tied to a manifestation by the actual principal of the mortgage interest. Here, the record described in the brief shows an informal, unfiled side arrangement—not evidence that Equity Trust manifested authority to Land Title or that Lundberg’s signature alone could bind the mortgagee as a matter of law. That is, at minimum, a disputed issue, not a summary-judgment certainty.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack on the alternative affirmance theory. Ohio apparent-authority law turns on manifestations traceable to the principal, not just the supposed agent’s own conduct, and the brief does not point to any manifestation from Equity Trust itself beyond the fact that Lundberg signed and handed over a release. The brief tries to recast the issue as whether Lundberg can deny his own authority years later, but that does not really answer the doctrinal problem that apparent authority ordinarily cannot be self-created.
challenges.suggested_response: The Court need not resolve a free-standing apparent-authority question to affirm. The undisputed record shows that Lundberg signed a written Release of Lien, delivered it for filing, and proceeded on the understanding that he would be repaid by other arrangements and would be an unsecured creditor. Whatever label is placed on his authority, or lack of it, the record does not show a compensable injury caused by Land Title’s accommodation filing.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow or drop the apparent-authority theory. The record cited in the brief does not show a manifestation by Equity Trust itself, so the brief should not rest affirmance on that doctrine; instead, it should say the Court need not resolve the authority label because Lundberg’s own signed release and expected unsecured status defeat causation.

challenges.opponent_argument: The 'if he can enforce it, he can release it' premise is not supported by the authority available here. Ohio Rev. Code 1309.203 makes enforceability turn on rights in the collateral or power to transfer those rights. The brief identifies Equity Trust as the named mortgagee and does not show that Lundberg, in his individual capacity, had the power to transfer the mortgage interest. Without that showing, the brief’s actual-authority alternative does not follow as a matter of law.
challenges.why_it_matters: This undercuts the second route to affirmance by showing the necessary transfer power was never established.

challenges.judge_assessment: The actual-authority fallback is vulnerable because the brief never shows that Eric Lundberg, in his individual capacity, had rights in the mortgage or power to transfer the mortgagee’s interest. The cited UCC-enforceability statute addresses when a security interest is enforceable, but it does not by itself prove that an IRA beneficiary or beneficial owner can release a mortgage held in Equity Trust’s name. If the court insists on proof of authority from the named mortgagee or a valid transfer power, this argument can fail.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Lundberg now contends that he lacked authority to act for Equity Trust, that contention does not change the result here. The undisputed record shows that he executed a written Release of Lien, delivered it for filing, and understood that the loan would be repaid by other arrangements. Land Title’s accommodation filing did not proximately cause a compensable injury because Lundberg was not left in any worse position than the one he voluntarily accepted.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not press the actual-authority fallback as a stand-alone matter of law unless the record contains a trust document, assignment, or power of attorney. The safer course is to remove that assertion and rely instead on Lundberg’s signed release and the no-proximate-cause analysis.

challenges.opponent_argument: The alternative standing theory goes too far. The cited Ohio standing cases say standing is a threshold question decided as a matter of law, but they do not hold that a person named in the pleadings as the beneficial owner of an IRA-held mortgage is automatically barred from suing for injury to that economic interest. The brief itself pleads that Lundberg acted individually and as beneficial owner of the IRA; the leap from custodial title in Equity Trust’s name to 'no standing at all' is not established by the authority the brief cites.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Lundberg can sue for his own asserted beneficial interest, Land Title loses its fallback affirmance ground.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real fallback attack, but it is not a clean winner on this record. The brief does cite standing cases and it does say Equity Trust, not Lundberg individually, is the mortgage holder, with no assignment or power of attorney produced. Still, the leap from named mortgagee to total lack of standing against Lundberg as beneficial owner is not fully demonstrated by the authorities the brief cites, so the court could view this as an overreach rather than an automatic bar.
challenges.suggested_response: If, as Lundberg argued below, Equity Trust Company is the named mortgagee and no assignment or power of attorney was produced, then Lundberg has not shown that he is authorized to assert Equity Trust’s mortgage rights in his individual capacity. On this record, he cannot invoke the mortgage when it benefits him and disclaim the mortgagee’s interest when it does not. At a minimum, he has not identified any evidence establishing that he may sue Land Title on Equity Trust’s behalf.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Soften the standing section. Do not say Lundberg has no standing at all unless the brief can tie that conclusion to a concrete authorization issue in the record; instead, say he has not produced any assignment, power of attorney, or other authority showing he may assert Equity Trust’s mortgage rights in his individual capacity.

challenges.opponent_argument: Land Title’s proximate-cause theory assumes, without legal support, that a signed but never-filed release is the functional equivalent of a recorded release. It is not enough to say Lundberg signed paper and expected to be unsecured; Ohio proximate cause still requires a reasonable connection between the challenged act and the claimed injury. On this record, the disputed question is whether Land Title’s accommodation filing itself is what kept the mortgage in the public record and caused the alleged harm. The brief does not eliminate that causal chain as a matter of law.
challenges.why_it_matters: If causation remains a factual question, summary judgment on the core theory cannot stand.

challenges.judge_assessment: The causation attack has some force, but the brief already has a substantial answer: Lundberg signed a release, gave it for filing, understood the loan would be repaid by other means, and would have been an unsecured creditor either way. On that record, the court can accept the brief’s position that the accommodation filing did not proximately cause a legally cognizable loss. The opponent’s point that an unfiled release is not the same as a recorded release is true in the abstract, but the attack does not tie that distinction to a concrete damages theory that survives the brief’s facts.
challenges.suggested_response: The dispositive question is not whether an unfiled release is the same thing as a recorded release in the abstract. It is whether Land Title’s accommodation filing proximately caused any cognizable injury to Lundberg. On the undisputed record, it did not. Lundberg signed a written Release of Lien, delivered it for filing, and understood that the loan would be repaid by other arrangements and that he would be an unsecured creditor. In light of that record, any injury he claims cannot be traced to Land Title’s accommodation filing as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the proximate-cause point, but tighten it around the undisputed facts that Lundberg signed a release, expected to be unsecured, and arranged to be repaid by other means. Do not frame the issue as if a signed-but-unfiled release is legally identical to a recorded one; frame it as a damages question that the record resolves against Lundberg.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates the evidence by treating the parties’ informal repayment plan as proof that Lundberg was in the same position regardless of Land Title’s filing. But the cited testimony shows only a private arrangement to keep the release in a file cabinet and use it later; it does not show an actual filed release, nor that the mortgage cloud would have existed or been harmless no matter what Land Title did. At minimum, that leaves a factual dispute on whether the accommodation filing caused the claimed injury.
challenges.why_it_matters: A genuine dispute over the effect of the filing defeats the 'no proximate cause as a matter of law' rationale.

challenges.judge_assessment: This mostly repackages a1. The cited testimony about keeping the release in a file cabinet and using it to make the property look over-encumbered actually helps the brief’s theory that Lundberg accepted the unsecured position and was not harmed by the filing in the way alleged. The attack does not identify a record fact showing a separate damages chain from Land Title’s filing, so it is unlikely to move the court.
challenges.suggested_response: The testimony does not create a genuine issue that matters to causation. Kevin Sheridan testified that the parties had worked out other arrangements to pay back the loan and that the purpose of the release was to take the mortgage off the house and leave Lundberg unsecured. That evidence confirms that Lundberg was already in the position he expected to occupy when he signed the release. On these facts, Land Title’s accommodation filing did not cause the alleged loss.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Use the existing testimony more carefully. The record cited in the brief supports the point that Lundberg and Kevin Sheridan had already worked out a different repayment arrangement and that the release was intended to make the property appear over-encumbered; that undercuts, rather than helps, a factual-dispute argument on causation.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief also overstates the reach of its cited causation cases by collapsing every claim into one undifferentiated proximate-cause theory. The authorities it invokes are general negligence/fraud/fiduciary-duty causation cases; they do not show that a separate notary-duty claim rises or falls on the same proof, or that Land Title is entitled to judgment on all theories simply because it thinks the parties expected an unsecured loan. On this briefing, that is too broad a jump.
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if one theory were weak, the brief does not establish that every claim is barred on the same rationale.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is mostly displaced by the brief itself. The brief and the trial court entry both say proximate cause is common to negligence, fraud, fiduciary-duty, and notary-duty claims, and the brief expressly includes the notary-duty theory in its no-proximate-cause discussion. So the notion that the brief ignored or overcollapsed the notary claim does not really land on this record. At most, it is a reminder that the court should verify each cause of action’s elements, but the brief already tries to do that by making proximate cause the common failure point.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court’s September 7, 2011 Journal Entry correctly recognized that, whether Lundberg’s claims sound in negligence, fraud, breach of fiduciary duty, or breach of duty as a notary, proximate cause of injury is a common element. Because the undisputed record shows that Lundberg signed the Release of Lien, expected to be unsecured, and has not shown any injury proximately caused by Land Title’s accommodation filing, summary judgment was proper on each of those claims.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the broad common-thread point, but anchor it in the trial court’s own entry and avoid sounding as though the case was decided by one catchall theory alone. Make clear that the same absence of proximate cause defeats each cause of action actually pleaded against Land Title.

attacks_proposed.argument: Land Title’s proximate-cause theory assumes, without legal support, that a signed but never-filed release is the functional equivalent of a recorded release. It is not enough to say Lundberg signed paper and expected to be unsecured; Ohio proximate cause still requires a reasonable connection between the challenged act and the claimed injury. On this record, the disputed question is whether Land Title’s accommodation filing itself is what kept the mortgage in the public record and caused the alleged harm. The brief does not eliminate that causal chain as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If causation remains a factual question, summary judgment on the core theory cannot stand.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief overstates the evidence by treating the parties’ informal repayment plan as proof that Lundberg was in the same position regardless of Land Title’s filing. But the cited testimony shows only a private arrangement to keep the release in a file cabinet and use it later; it does not show an actual filed release, nor that the mortgage cloud would have existed or been harmless no matter what Land Title did. At minimum, that leaves a factual dispute on whether the accommodation filing caused the claimed injury.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A genuine dispute over the effect of the filing defeats the 'no proximate cause as a matter of law' rationale.

attacks_proposed.argument: The alternative standing theory goes too far. The cited Ohio standing cases say standing is a threshold question decided as a matter of law, but they do not hold that a person named in the pleadings as the beneficial owner of an IRA-held mortgage is automatically barred from suing for injury to that economic interest. The brief itself pleads that Lundberg acted individually and as beneficial owner of the IRA; the leap from custodial title in Equity Trust’s name to 'no standing at all' is not established by the authority the brief cites.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Lundberg can sue for his own asserted beneficial interest, Land Title loses its fallback affirmance ground.

attacks_proposed.argument: The 'if he can enforce it, he can release it' premise is not supported by the authority available here. Ohio Rev. Code 1309.203 makes enforceability turn on rights in the collateral or power to transfer those rights. The brief identifies Equity Trust as the named mortgagee and does not show that Lundberg, in his individual capacity, had the power to transfer the mortgage interest. Without that showing, the brief’s actual-authority alternative does not follow as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This undercuts the second route to affirmance by showing the necessary transfer power was never established.

attacks_proposed.argument: Land Title’s apparent-authority theory is also incomplete. The brief relies on Kevin Sheridan’s subjective understanding of a private repayment arrangement, but subjective belief does not supply the missing legal link unless it is tied to a manifestation by the actual principal of the mortgage interest. Here, the record described in the brief shows an informal, unfiled side arrangement—not evidence that Equity Trust manifested authority to Land Title or that Lundberg’s signature alone could bind the mortgagee as a matter of law. That is, at minimum, a disputed issue, not a summary-judgment certainty.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If apparent authority is not established conclusively, Land Title cannot use estoppel to short-circuit the merits.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief also overstates the reach of its cited causation cases by collapsing every claim into one undifferentiated proximate-cause theory. The authorities it invokes are general negligence/fraud/fiduciary-duty causation cases; they do not show that a separate notary-duty claim rises or falls on the same proof, or that Land Title is entitled to judgment on all theories simply because it thinks the parties expected an unsecured loan. On this briefing, that is too broad a jump.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if one theory were weak, the brief does not establish that every claim is barred on the same rationale.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack on the alternative affirmance theory. Ohio apparent-authority law turns on manifestations traceable to the principal, not just the supposed agent’s own conduct, and the brief does not point to any manifestation from Equity Trust itself beyond the fact that Lundberg signed and handed over a release. The brief tries to recast the issue as whether Lundberg can deny his own authority years later, but that does not really answer the doctrinal problem that apparent authority ordinarily cannot be self-created.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It argues that Lundberg’s words and conduct, plus Kevin Sheridan’s understanding of their arrangement, reasonably led Sheridan to believe Lundberg had authority, and it quotes Master Consol. and Miller for binding a party by apparent authority or estoppel.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Master Consol. and related Ohio authority on whose manifestations count for apparent authority would decide whether Equity Trust’s absence is fatal.

judge_assessments.assessment: The actual-authority fallback is vulnerable because the brief never shows that Eric Lundberg, in his individual capacity, had rights in the mortgage or power to transfer the mortgagee’s interest. The cited UCC-enforceability statute addresses when a security interest is enforceable, but it does not by itself prove that an IRA beneficiary or beneficial owner can release a mortgage held in Equity Trust’s name. If the court insists on proof of authority from the named mortgagee or a valid transfer power, this argument can fail.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says that if Lundberg can enforce the lien, he can release it, and it relies on the release document’s caption naming Equity Trust Company, Custodian FBO Eric Lundberg IRA, plus Lundberg’s signature and the parties’ course of dealing.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The record would need evidence of Equity Trust’s authorization, assignment, or a power of attorney to make this fallback solid.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real fallback attack, but it is not a clean winner on this record. The brief does cite standing cases and it does say Equity Trust, not Lundberg individually, is the mortgage holder, with no assignment or power of attorney produced. Still, the leap from named mortgagee to total lack of standing against Lundberg as beneficial owner is not fully demonstrated by the authorities the brief cites, so the court could view this as an overreach rather than an automatic bar.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It expressly says Lundberg cannot take inconsistent positions, that only Equity Trust has standing if Equity Trust is the mortgage holder, that Equity Trust is not a party, and that no assignment or power of attorney was produced.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether a beneficial owner/IRA beneficiary may sue for injury to the mortgage interest would settle this.

judge_assessments.assessment: The causation attack has some force, but the brief already has a substantial answer: Lundberg signed a release, gave it for filing, understood the loan would be repaid by other means, and would have been an unsecured creditor either way. results.assessment: The brief is strongest on proximate cause: the record facts it relies on support the point that Lundberg signed the release, expected to be unsecured, and has not shown a separate injury from Land Title’s accommodation filing. Its biggest weakness is the alternative authority theory. The brief does not supply a clear manifestation from Equity Trust, so apparent authority is vulnerable, and the leap from named mortgagee to Lundberg’s individual authority or standing is not well supported. The causation discussion also needs tighter handling of the distinction between a signed but unfiled release and a recorded release, because that gap is the cleanest remaining attack.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. On the brief's own presentation, the summary-judgment argument is largely conclusory: it asserts the dispositive facts (no legal marriage, mother paid the bill, cremains were buried, appellant defaulted) and cites exhibits, but the record provided here does not contain those exhibits or any developed evidentiary showing. Under the Rule 56 authorities cited, the moving party must establish entitlement as a matter of law and the absence of a genuine factual dispute; this brief does not actually demonstrate that on the face of the supplied record. The brief partly answers by asserting the facts are 'uncontroverted,' but that is not the same as showing admissible evidence. Appellee risks losing the summary-judgment affirmance.
challenges.suggested_response: The record before the trial court included sworn affidavits and documentary exhibits supporting appellee's position, and appellant filed no counter-evidence after receiving an extension of time to respond. Under Civ.R. 56 and the Temple/Mers standard, summary judgment was proper because no genuine issue of material fact remained and appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make the Civ.R. 56 analysis evidence-based. Tie the result to the sworn materials and the lack of any counter-evidence, and avoid simply repeating the conclusion that appellee was entitled to judgment.

challenges.opponent_argument: The sanctions request is underdeveloped and therefore cannot support reversal. The brief lists multiple cases and describes appellant's conduct in pejorative terms, but it never sets out the statutory elements of R.C. 2323.52 in a disciplined way or explains how each listed filing satisfies them. A list of lawsuits, without a record-based showing that the conduct was unwarranted under existing law and undertaken without a good-faith basis, is not enough to compel a vexatious-litigant designation.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the statutory elements are not actually proven, the denial of sanctions should stand.

target.excerpt: V. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN FAILING TO GRANT DEFENDANT'S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS. WHICH INCLUDED DECLARING PLAINTIFF. WILFRED LOUIS ANDERSON. A VEXATIOUS LITIGATOR AS THAT TERM IS DEFINED IN OHIO REVISED CODE SECTION 2323.52.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack lands in part. R.C. 2323.52 is the right statute, and repeated filings in multiple forums can support a vexatious-litigant finding, but the brief does not do the statutory work: it does not clearly organize the elements, specify the required standard of proof, or tie each cited filing to the statutory definitions with record support. The brief does answer somewhat by listing several cases and alleging harassment, but the submission reads more like accusation than a developed statutory analysis. Appellee stands to lose the sanctions request if the court insists on a proper element-by-element showing.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 2323.52 is aimed at a litigant who habitually engages in vexatious conduct. The record identified in this brief shows appellant filing the same core dispute in multiple forums, including the concurrent Summit County action, the Cuyahoga County action, the prior appeal, the Court of Claims matter, and related proceedings against the City of Cleveland Heights and the Cleveland Heights Police Department, after he had already been warned to stop harassing appellee. That pattern supports the vexatious-litigant finding and sanctions requested below.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Rebuild the sanctions section around the statutory standard and the concrete filing history. State the repeated filings in the same controversy, but do not rely on rhetoric alone; if the record does not contain docket entries or the statute's full elements, say less rather than more.

challenges.opponent_argument: The 'no forgery' point is not established by the material the brief identifies. The brief relies on the notary's licensing status on January 9, 2013, but a valid commission proves only authority to notarize; it does not prove the signature was genuine. With no case record supplied here, the assertion that there was 'no evidence' of forgery is just advocacy, not evidentiary support.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without actual proof negating forgery, the fraud-upon-the-court theory remains unresolved and cannot be rejected on this record.

target.excerpt: II. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN FAILING TO FIND DEFENDANT COMMITED FRAUD UPON THE COURT WHEN THE NOTARY SIGNATURE APPEARING IN DEFENDANT'S PLEADING WAS NOT FORGED.

challenges.judge_assessment: The point that a valid commission does not prove the signature was genuine is correct, and the brief does not supply independent evidence negating forgery beyond saying the notary was licensed on the date of notarization. That means the 'no forgery' conclusion is asserted, not demonstrated. The brief partly answers by saying the notary was duly licensed and empowered at the time, but licensing status is not the same as proof that the signature on the affidavit was not forged. On this record, the fraud-upon-the-court argument is not fully extinguished by the cited materials alone.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant's commission argument does not establish forgery. The materials identified show that the notary was duly licensed on the date of notarization and that the affidavits were properly sworn, but appellant points to no record evidence proving that the notary's signature was forged. The trial court therefore did not err in declining to find fraud upon the court.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Remove the absolute statement that the notary signature was not forged unless the record actually proves that fact. Recast the argument as one about appellant's failure to produce evidence of forgery.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 147. Its own discussion only shows that the affidavit was sworn before a licensed notary and that a seal was affixed; that goes to notarization mechanics, not to whether the underlying filing was false, fabricated, or otherwise fraudulent. Chapter 147 does not supply the missing legal bridge from 'properly notarized' to 'cannot be fraud upon the court.'
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court accepts that false bridge, any fraud challenge collapses whenever a commission exists, even if the underlying affidavit is otherwise suspect.

target.excerpt: I. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN FAILING TO FIND DEFENDANT COMMITTED FRAUD UPON THE COURT WHEN DEFENDANT SUBMITTED AN AFFIDAVIT SIGNED BY A LICENSED NOTARY IN THE STATE OF OHIO.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real but narrower flaw. The brief cites R.C. 147 for ordinary notarization principles, but Chapter 147 by itself does not establish the critical legal proposition that any affidavit signed before a licensed notary cannot, as a matter of law, amount to fraud upon the court. The brief answers only the notarization mechanics: licensed notary, seal affixed, certification on the document. It does not supply the fraud standard or explain why proper notarization defeats a fraud theory in all circumstances. Appellee risks overclaiming the effect of the statute.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. Ohio Civ.R. 56 does not allow judgment simply because the nonmovant failed to file a response; the movant still must show no genuine issue and entitlement as a matter of law, with evidence viewed most strongly for the nonmovant. The brief partly tries to pivot to the merits by saying the motion was "well-taken" and the court reviewed the record, but it also squarely relies on waiver/failure to respond as a justification. An Ohio appellate court would not treat silence as a substitute for proof. If this is the foundation for affirmance, the appellee risks reversal or remand on the summary-judgment assignment.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s failure to file a response did not relieve the trial court of its duty to decide the motion under Civ.R. 56. The court nevertheless reviewed the materials submitted, and those materials established no genuine issue of material fact and entitled Defendant to judgment as a matter of law. The judgment was proper not because Appellant remained silent, but because the evidence before the court supported only one conclusion.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Remove the suggestion that Appellant’s silence itself justified judgment. Recast the paragraph to say that the trial court still had to decide the motion under Civ.R. 56, and that after reviewing the materials before it, the court properly found no genuine issue of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law.

The retrieved authority indicates the statute requires more than repeated filings in different courts; it calls for the same-matter showing, a good-faith analysis, and the statutory procedure, including notice, hearing, and specific findings. challenges.judge_assessment: This is the best attack on the mootness theory. The cited materials discuss stays, supersedeas, and post-execution remedies, but they do not clearly establish that simply recording a certified copy of a quiet-title judgment is the same thing as executing it for mootness purposes. On this record, the brief’s leap from recordation to mootness is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: A. The Stovalls do not even challenge the Eighth District's decision that their appeal is moot. Indeed, they concede that Lender recorded a certified copy of the quiet-title judgment before they filed their notice of appeal or sought a stay. The trial court later denied their stay motion as moot because Lender had "already executed judgment," and the Eighth District dismissed the appeal on the same ground. On this record, the appeal was moot when filed because the judgment had already been carried into effect before any stay was sought.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not treat recordation alone as a universal execution rule. Recast the mootness point as a record-specific one: the trial court found the judgment had already been executed before any stay motion, the Stovalls appealed only after that occurred, and the Eighth District dismissed on that basis.

The cited eviction authorities contemplate relief after execution in some settings, so the proposition that no effective relief remains is not automatic. challenges.suggested_response: The Stovalls also identify no effective relief that would remain available even if this Court were to revisit the merits. The authorities they invoke discuss stays, supersedeas bonds, and, in possession cases, return-to-possession remedies after a writ has already issued. Those authorities do not show that a quiet-title appeal remains justiciable after the judgment has already been executed and recorded. The Stovalls have pointed to no Ohio authority that would allow this Court to grant them meaningful relief on these facts, so the appeal would be purely academic.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the "purely academic" point. Say that the cited stay-and-return authorities are possession cases and do not show a live remedy for this recorded quiet-title judgment, so the Stovalls have identified no effective relief this Court could grant.

They had notice and a fair opportunity to be heard: they could have conducted discovery, filed evidence, and responded meaningfully to summary judgment. results.assessment: The brief reads strongest where it ties mootness to the record: the Stovalls concede recordation before appeal, and they offered no clear route to meaningful relief on these facts. But it overstates the law by treating recordation as though it were plainly the same as execution, when the challenged authorities do not cleanly make that leap. The “purely academic” point is also broader than the record supports, because the cited materials contemplate post-execution relief in possession cases. The due-process and summary-judgment attacks are weaker: the record emphasizes notice, an opportunity to respond, sworn affidavits, and no countervailing evidence, which leaves those challenges looking thin.

challenges.opponent_argument: The mootness theory overstates Ohio law. The authorities in the brief show that when a party wants to enforce an eviction-type judgment during an appeal, the ordinary issue is whether a stay or supersedeas bond should issue—not whether the appeal disappears the moment enforcement begins. That is exactly how the cited materials treat execution pending appeal: they discuss stays of execution and supersedeas bonds, which presuppose a live appeal even after judgment enforcement is sought. On this record, the mere fact that Lender recorded a certified copy of the judgment does not, by itself, establish that the appeal became moot.
challenges.why_it_matters: If recording the judgment is not automatic mootness, the Court cannot dismiss jurisdiction solely on that ground and must confront the appealability question on the merits.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. The brief assumes that recording a certified copy of the judgment counts as execution and therefore moots the appeal, but the cited authorities in the brief do not themselves establish that proposition on this record. The attack also has a real procedural point: the stay/supersedeas materials show the ordinary response to enforcement is a stay request, which suggests a live appeal can still exist. If the court rejects the execution=mootness step, the brief loses its threshold jurisdictional ground and the court may have to confront the merits or another jurisdictional basis.
challenges.suggested_response: A. The Stovalls do not meaningfully challenge the Eighth District's mootness holding. They concede that Lender recorded a certified copy of the judgment before they filed their notice of appeal or moved to stay, and the trial court later denied their stay motion as moot because Lender had already executed the judgment. See Mem. at 2; R. 46. At minimum, the Stovalls identify no live controversy this Court can remedy, and they have forfeited any developed argument to the contrary by failing to raise it in their jurisdictional memorandum. In any event, none of the issues they raise presents a matter of public and great general interest or a substantial constitutional question.

Tighten the paragraph to the facts actually in the record: the judgment had already been recorded, the trial court later denied a stay as moot, and the Stovalls did not squarely preserve any developed mootness challenge in their jurisdictional memorandum. Keep the alternative point that, even if the Court looks past mootness, the case presents no issue of public and great general interest or substantial constitutional question.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack because it goes to the core legal theory: whether SB 97 governs the January 1, 2002 renewal and eliminates any basis for implied UM/UIM coverage. The brief does not ignore the point; it cites Arn, Advent, McDaniel, St. Clair, and Storer, and it expressly acknowledges a certified conflict and a pending Ohio Supreme Court question. That means the issue was not settled beyond dispute, but it was still open enough for the appellate court to follow the line of cases Westport cites. So the attack lands as a real merits challenge, not a knockout punch. Westport would lose the argument only if the panel rejected the renewal-incorporation cases it relies on.
challenges.suggested_response: Even though the parties have noted a certified conflict on the renewal-incorporation question, this Court need not treat the issue as unresolved for purposes of this appeal. The authorities Westport cites, including Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, hold that statutory changes may be incorporated into a renewal policy during the two-year guaranteed period and that the law in effect at renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage. Here, Senate Bill 97 was effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal, and the policy was renewed after that enactment. Under those authorities, the January 1, 2002 renewal governed, and Ohio law did not require an offer of UM/UIM coverage or permit such coverage to be implied by operation of law on the July 15, 2002 date of loss.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not overstate SB 97 as settled law. Recast this point as an application of the appellate authorities you already cite, while acknowledging the certified conflict and explaining why Westport is asking this Court to follow Arn, Advent, and St. Clair on the facts here. If the brief cannot obtain a more definitive authority, it should say only that those cases support affirmance, not that the issue is beyond dispute.

That means the issue was not settled beyond dispute, but it was still open enough for the appellate court to follow the line of cases Westport cites. So the attack lands as a real merits challenge, not a knockout punch. Westport would lose the argument only if the panel rejected the renewal-incorporation cases it relies on.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Senate Bill 97 became effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal; under Arn and Advent, statutory changes could be incorporated at renewal; the brief acknowledges Storer and the certified conflict, but argues the law in effect at renewal governs and UM/UIM could not be implied by operation of law on the July 15, 2002 loss date.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The then-controlling Ohio Supreme Court resolution of the Advent/Storer conflict and whether it applied to renewals like this one.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is not a strong record attack. The brief does not merely assert a conclusion; it says the excess policy provides only sums in excess of primary insurance or a retained limit and that it is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary insurance. That is enough, on this record, to support the trial court’s treatment of the excess form unless appellants identify a policy provision creating a separate UM/UIM obligation. The opponent’s point is that Westport did not quote the exact exclusionary language, but summary judgment does not fail just because the brief paraphrases the policy rather than reproducing every clause.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The Commercial Excess Policy provides excess coverage above primary insurance or a retained limit, is subject to the same terms and limitations as the primary policy, and the trial court found it need not provide UM/UIM coverage where the underlying policies do not.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is not supported by the cited source. The brief’s SB97 argument is anchored in Arn, Advent, McDaniel, St. Clair, Storer, and Shay, and it quotes the amended statute and the renewal rule. The attack’s reliance on source 21 is not a fit on its face and does not supply a contrary insurance-renewal rule. More importantly, the brief already answers the point by arguing that SB97 was effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal and that coverage could not then be implied by operation of law. On this record, the court would likely consider the cited authorities the relevant ones and reject the attack as unsupported and off-point.
challenges.suggested_response: Senate Bill 97 went into effect on October 31, 2001, before the Westport policies renewed on January 1, 2002. Under Arn v. McLean, at the time of that renewal Westport did not have to offer or include UM/UIM coverage, and such coverage could no longer be implied by operation of law. Advent and St. Clair likewise recognize that statutory changes in effect at renewal govern the scope of UM/UIM coverage. Accordingly, plaintiffs cannot avoid SB97 by pointing to an earlier bind date when the operative policy period in this case renewed after SB97 became law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the SB97 argument, but tighten it around the actual renewal date and the cases the brief already cites. Do not rely on source 21; instead, state directly that the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, after SB97 took effect, and that Arn, Advent, and St. Clair make the law at renewal control the scope of UM/UIM coverage.

Because Westport asks the court to decide the effect of Senate Bill 97 by rule rather than by contract-specific evidence, it asks for more than the record as presented can support.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the December 2000 binding period controls, SB97’s effective date before the 2002 renewal does not end the coverage analysis, and Westport loses the clean statutory cutoff it relies on.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport’s excess-policy argument is underdeveloped. The brief does not cite controlling authority establishing that a commercial excess policy can never carry separate UM/UIM obligations; it simply assumes the excess form follows the underlying auto and general liability policies for all purposes. But the summary-judgment record described here does not contain a full policy-text analysis proving that the excess form lacks its own UM/UIM obligation. Without that, Westport has not shown entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the excess policy.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the excess form is not conclusively derivative of the underlying forms, plaintiffs’ excess-policy claim survives even if Westport prevails on some arguments about the primary auto policy.

judge_assessments.assessment: This does not land as a real record problem. The brief already concedes there was no physical printout for the first month and says a binder was issued for that period; it then explains that the January 1, 2001 and January 1, 2002 policies were produced and that no Westport policy was withheld. Source 41 is only a generic missing-policy/binder reference and source 79 is just the summary-judgment standard; neither shows that a binder, standing alone, creates a genuine dispute defeating Westport’s coverage defense. On this record, the court would likely treat this as a discovery complaint, not a merits defect. Westport loses little unless plaintiffs can identify a specific missing policy term that changes the coverage analysis.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: No physical policies were printed for December 1, 2000 to January 1, 2001; a binder evidenced that period; later policies were produced; and it is untrue that any Westport policy was not produced.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Only a specific missing contract term or admissible evidence of an unproduced operative policy would change this.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief does not leave the governing policy period unresolved. It identifies the January 1, 2002 to January 1, 2003 policy as the policy at issue and supports the out-of-state delivery and garaging facts with the policy exhibits. The binder discussion does not create a separate statutory issue, because the argument is that R.C. 3937.18 never applied to these policies in the first place. Source 41 does not establish a contrary rule, and source 79 does not convert a bare binder objection into a factual dispute on the statute’s geographic prerequisites. A court on this record would likely reject this as a reargument of discovery, not a genuine issue of material fact.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The policies at issue were produced; the January 1, 2002 to January 1, 2003 policy is identified as the operative policy; and the policies were issued in Kansas to a Pennsylvania insured with Florida and Pennsylvania vehicles, not Ohio ones.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A different result would require evidence that a different policy period or different vehicle location facts controlled the loss.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is not supported by the cited source. The brief’s SB97 argument is anchored in Arn, Advent, McDaniel, St. Clair, Storer, and Shay, and it quotes the amended statute and the renewal rule. The attack’s reliance on source 21 is not a fit on its face and does not supply a contrary insurance-renewal rule. More importantly, the brief already answers the point by arguing that SB97 was effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal and that coverage could not then be implied by operation of law. On this record, the court would likely consider the cited authorities the relevant ones and reject the attack as unsupported and off-point.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: SB97 was effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal; Arn says UM/UIM could no longer be implied by operation of law and no longer needed an offer or rejection form; Advent and St. Clair are cited for incorporation at renewal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: To change the result, plaintiffs would need controlling Ohio authority holding SB97 could not be incorporated at that renewal.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the same timing objection in different clothing, and it fares no better. The brief expressly states that coverage was first bound on December 1, 2000, that SB97 became effective October 31, 2001, and that it was incorporated when the policy renewed on January 1, 2002. The attack relies on the premise that the December 2000 bind date freezes the law, but the brief already addresses that with the renewal authorities. Source 63 is the statutory text, not a contrary rule, and source 21 does not supply one. On this record, the court would likely see no basis to bypass the renewal analysis Westport cites.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: December 1, 2000 inception; January 1, 2001 and January 1, 2002 renewals; SB97 effective October 31, 2001; law at renewal governs scope of UM/UIM coverage under the cited cases.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Only a controlling case squarely rejecting incorporation of SB97 at a renewal during the guaranteed period would move this.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the most substantial attack, but it still does not carry on this record. Westport’s brief gives a contractual answer: the excess policy is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary auto policy, and Westport says the underlying policies do not supply UM/UIM coverage. The attack is right that the brief does not cite a direct Ohio authority saying an excess policy can never have separate UM/UIM obligations, but that omission matters only if plaintiffs can point to policy language or authority showing an independent excess obligation. They do not do so here. If the court reaches the issue, Westport still has the stronger record position; if the statutory arguments fail, this could become the more vulnerable link.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The excess policy follows the primary auto policy for automobile liability, provides sums in excess of primary insurance or a retained limit, and Westport says no UM/UIM coverage exists in the underlying policies.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A complete analysis would require the full excess-policy text and Ohio authority on follow-form umbrella/excess UM/UIM coverage.
